subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Sunk Cost Trap
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Sunk Cost Trap.

hook.text: You've watched 90 minutes of a terrible movie. You stay because you 'already invested the time.'

buildup.text: Sunk costs are past expenses that can't be recovered. Logically, they shouldn't affect future decisions.

discovery.text: But abandoning feels like accepting a loss. Loss aversion makes us throw good resources after bad ones.

twist.text: Governments continue failing projects for the same reason. 'We've spent too much to stop now' is the trap's motto.

climax.text: Ask only: what are the future costs and benefits? Past spending is gone. Only the path forward matters.

punchline.text: What you've spent is spent. Decide from now.

quiz.question: Why do people fall into the sunk cost trap?
options: They want to maximize future returns
Abandoning past investment feels like accepting a loss

details.summary: The sunk cost trap is the tendency to continue investing in a losing proposition because of what has already been spent, even when the rational choice is to cut losses. Past investments should be irrelevant to forward-looking decisions, but loss aversion makes them sticky.
details.whyItMatters: Sunk cost reasoning wastes billions in business, government, and personal finance. Projects continue because too much has been invested to stop, even when stopping immediately would minimize total losses.
takeaways: Past spending should not influence future decisions but consistently does
Abandoning an investment feels like confirming a loss, triggering loss aversion
The Concorde supersonic jet is the classic example of sunk cost escalation

faq.question: Why is the Concorde the classic sunk cost example?
faq.answer: Britain and France continued funding the Concorde long after it was clear it would never be commercially viable. Billions already spent made stopping feel like wasting that investment, so they spent billions more on a project that lost money until retirement.

faq.question: How can you overcome sunk cost thinking?
faq.answer: Ask: if I were starting fresh today with no prior investment, would I choose this option? If no, the sunk costs are trapping you. Seek outside opinions from people who are not emotionally invested in the prior spending.
